chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Asbat ibn Salim who said:
I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he asked us about Umar ibn Muslim, saying, 'What has become of him?' We said, 'He is good, but he has left trade.'

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'His action is that of the Shaytan (in a negative sense of neglecting duty for a specific reason, or perhaps 'three things' refers to a broader context not fully quoted here, but the core is the Prophet's trade). Do you not know that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) bought a caravan that came from Syria, and he profited from it, paid off his debt, and distributed among his relatives.'
Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah and the performance of prayer' until the end of the verse.

The storytellers say that the people (of the verse) did not trade at all; they are lying. But rather, they did not abandon prayer at its appointed time. And they are superior to those who attended prayer but did not trade.

key_terms.عِيرًا: A caravan of goods or camels

ai.seo_question: Does Islam prohibit trade and business for Muslims according to the Quranic verse about 'Men whom neither trade nor sale diverts...?'
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the Quranic verse (24:37) criticizes those whose trade *prevents* them from praying, not those who trade but still maintain their prayer on time. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) engaged in trade (buying a caravan from Syria) to pay debts and give to his family, yet he was not 'diverted' from prayer. Thus, trading is permissible and praiseworthy as long as it does not neglect the obligatory prayers.
